Mobile app · Fintech

PaisaWise mobile app design

An AI-native UPI spend tracker for India. It gives you one daily limit, a live “left today” number from your bank SMS, and an assistant you can ask out loud. It helps young earners see the small payments before they add up.

RoleProduct Design
Duration6 weeks
ProjectMobile App (concept)
IndustryFintech
ToolsFigma, Miro, ChatGPT, Claude
PlatformAndroid & iOS

Self-initiated concept · not affiliated with any bank, NPCI or UPI app

The result

A spend tracker that answers “Am I okay today?” before the month is over, without any manual entry.

  • One daily limit, always liveEvery UPI payment is read from bank SMS and taken off today’s number.
  • Support instead of blameAn overspent day comes with a way back, not a red lecture.
  • A voice agent you can talk toPlay the voice agent demo and listen: ask out loud where your money went and PaisaWise answers in one sentence. It is read-only and can never move money.

Expected impact

What I expect to change

↑

Days within limit

40%+

of days within the limit by month 2

How I got this: The limit is set from your own last 30 days, so about half of days already land under it. 40% is a careful start while habits form.

↑

Auto-tracking

90%+

of UPI payments caught without typing

How I got this: Bank SMS covers UPI from every app. A few payments send no SMS or an odd format, so I didn’t assume 100%.

↑

Day-30 retention

6%+

still opening the app after 30 days

How I got this: Finance apps keep about 2% (Adjust) to 8% (OneSignal) of users by day 30. 6% is ambitious but inside that real range.

↑

Ask PaisaWise

70%+

of answers marked helpful

How I got this: Answers come from your own payments, not guesses. 70% leaves room for misheard questions early on.

Launch targets, not results · the app isn’t live yet. I’ll check each one in a 2-week Android pilot.

Problem

Why people lose track of UPI spending

01

Small payments don’t feel like spending

₹20 for tea and ₹60 for the metro feel like nothing. Many of them together can be more than you planned to spend that day.

02

You find out too late

Bank apps and statements show what already happened. By month end, there’s nothing left to change.

03

Tracking is a chore

Typing in every payment works for a week. Then people stop, and the app becomes useless.

04

Looking feels bad

Red warnings and “you overspent” make people feel judged, so they avoid opening the app at all.

Phase 01

Discover & research

How I found the problem

Market researchCompetitor analysisWhat users say
01
1

Step 01Market research

View full image

I started with public payment data to check whether “many small payments” is a real, everyday pattern, or just how I pay.

  1. 01

    UPI is huge and still growing. 25.47 billion payments in October 2026, about 822 million a day, up about 23% on the year before.

  2. 02

    Most shop payments are small. 86% of person-to-merchant UPI payments in FY2025-26 were under ₹500.

  3. 03

    Payments are getting smaller. The average UPI payment fell from ₹1,515 (H2 2023) to ₹1,314 (2025), as everyday purchases moved to UPI.

✦ Key insight

The problem isn’t one big purchase. It’s many small ones spread across the day. So a daily number fits how people really pay better than a monthly budget does.

2

Step 02Competitor analysis

View full image

I compared six products Indians use to see their spending, using their websites, app listings and news coverage.

  1. 01

    Daily limit: 0 of 6. Every budget I found is monthly. BHIM’s monthly budget comes closest.

  2. 02

    Payment apps only see themselves. Paytm and BHIM show spending made through their own app, but most people use more than one UPI app.

  3. 03

    Most free trackers sell something else. Axio now belongs to Amazon’s lending arm and ET Money to a wealth manager. Fold charges ₹2,999 a year instead.

✦ Opportunity

No one is giving people a live, daily view across all their UPI apps. That gap matters, because UPI spending happens day by day.

3

Step 03What users say

View full image

Source: a 2024 IIIT Delhi study of UPI users: a survey (235 valid answers), 20 follow-up interviews and a usability test with 34 people. It is self-reported and urban, so I read it as a signal, not proof.

  1. 01

    People feel UPI makes them spend more. 74.2% said their spending went up; 59.8% admitted to overspending.

  2. 02

    They want to see it. 87.9% wanted an expense tracker inside the app, and 78.8% wanted to see their balance before and after paying.

  3. 03

    They don’t want to be slowed down. Only 24.2% liked the idea of a timer that delays payments.

✦ Key insight

People don’t want to be stopped. They want to see. The design should show spending clearly and early, and never block a payment.

Define & design

Step 01Affinity mapping

3public data sourcesNPCI, Worldline, PIB · UPI volumes and payment sizes
6products comparedAxio, CRED Money, Fold, Paytm, BHIM, ET Money
1user studyIIIT Delhi, 2024 · 235 survey answers, 34 in a usability test

I grouped every finding by the need behind it. Seven struggles came up, and each one points to one of three ideas.

1Small payments feel free86% of shop payments are under ₹500Daily limit
2Monthly budgets come too lateEvery tracker found works monthlyDaily limit
3Spending is split across appsPaytm and BHIM only see themselvesDaily limit
4Manual entry gets droppedFinance apps keep ~2% after 30 daysDaily limit
5Warnings feel like judgementPeople avoid looking when it hurtsSupportive plan
6No way back after a bad dayAn overspent day just stays redSupportive plan
7Simple questions take many taps“What was this ₹499?”Ask PaisaWise
✦ Key insight

People aren’t careless with money. They just can’t see the small payments in time, and looking feels bad. The daily limit covers struggles 1–4, a supportive plan covers 5–6, and Ask PaisaWise covers 7.

2

Step 02Persona

View full image

I wrote a proto-persona from the research to keep my decisions focused on one person. Priya isn’t a real participant. She stands for the young, salaried UPI user the data describes.

  1. 01

    Priya Sharma, 27, is a product analyst in Bengaluru. She pays for almost everything with UPI across two apps, and orders food a few times a week.

  2. 02

    She wants to save ₹5,000 a month for an emergency fund and a trip, but she only sees what went wrong at month end. She has given up on two budget apps because of manual entry.

✦ Key insight

Priya doesn’t need more charts. She needs one number she can trust today, and zero effort to keep it up to date.

3

Step 03Empathy map

View full image

I mapped what Priya says, thinks, does and feels, to find the gap between her words and her actions.

  1. 01

    Says: “I’m not a big spender.” “I’ll start budgeting next month.”

  2. 02

    Thinks: “₹150 is nothing.” “Checking will only make me feel bad.”

  3. 03

    Does: pays 2–4 times a day, ignores small bank SMS, and drops budget apps after a week.

  4. 04

    Feels: guilty at month end, judged by red warnings, and calm when she knows exactly where she stands.

✦ Key insight

She avoids looking because looking hurts. Researchers call this the ostrich effect. So the app has to make checking feel safe: plain numbers, no blame, and always a next step.

4

Step 04User journey

One Thursday with a ₹500 daily limit. Six small payments add up to ₹778. Today she would only see it weeks later. I marked where PaisaWise steps in at each moment.

View full image
✦ Key insight

The moment that matters is 5:30 pm, when she has used 80% and can still change course. A gentle note there is worth more than a red alert at 10:20 pm or a statement in two weeks.

5

Step 05Information architecture

View full image

I built the app around five tabs, and each one answers one plain question.

  1. 01

    Home: “Am I okay today?” Left today, this week, today’s payments.

  2. 02

    Spends: “Where did it go?” Search, categories, payment details and the monthly report.

  3. 03

    Ask: “Just tell me.” Voice or text, read-only, in the centre of the bar.

  4. 04

    Wealth and Goals: “What do I own?” and “What is it for?” FDs, mutual funds, insurance and saving goals.

✦ Key insight

Daily spending comes first, and wealth comes second. Most people open a money app for today, so investments sit one tab away and don’t compete with the number that matters.

6

Step 06Wireframes

I sketched 13 low-fidelity screens in grey to fix the order of information before any colour. Numbered notes on each screen explain the choice.

View full image
✦ What changed after wireframes

My first version asked for Account Aggregator consent first. It took more steps and AA data isn’t real-time, so bank SMS became the recommended option, with Account Aggregator marked “Later” for investments.

“How might we”

Three questions that shaped the design

01

How might we

show small payments adding up, while it’s still today?

What I didOne daily limit with a live “left today” number.

02

How might we

help after a bad day without making people feel judged?

What I didA plain over-limit card with a plan to recover.

03

How might we

answer money questions in seconds, safely?

What I didAsk PaisaWise: a read-only voice assistant.

Solution

What I proposed

Three ideas, each linked to a finding, and each with a safety net if something goes wrong.

01

A live daily limit

WhyPayments are small and spread across the day, and monthly budgets come too late.

How it works

  1. Allow bank SMS once
  2. Pick a daily limit (suggested from your last 30 days)
  3. Every UPI payment lowers “left today”

Safety netRent, EMIs and SIPs are kept out, and any payment can be moved out of the limit.

02

A way back, and a reason to save

WhyBlame makes people stop looking, and an overspent day has no next step today.

How it works

  1. A note at 80% of the limit
  2. Over? See where it went, plainly
  3. Spread it over the next days, or keep the limit

Safety netUnspent money can go to goals, but only after you confirm. Nothing moves on its own.

03

Ask PaisaWise

WhySimple questions like “What was this ₹499?” take many taps, or a call to the bank.

How it works

  1. Tap Ask in the centre of the bar
  2. Speak or type a question
  3. Get a short answer with the numbers on screen

Safety netRead-only: it can’t pay or move money. Unknown debits show the 1930 cyber-crime helpline and your bank first.

Data & trust

Decisions I made to earn trust

A money app asks for very personal data. These were the trade-offs I chose on purpose.

01

Data source

Bank SMS now, Account Aggregator later

WhySMS is the only real-time source for a live daily number. Google Play allows SMS access for budgeting apps only after review, and iOS can’t read SMS, so AA is the planned second path.

02

Permissions

Read-only, everywhere

WhyPaisaWise never asks for UPI PINs or OTPs and can’t move money. The voice assistant can only answer and suggest.

03

Control

Your data stays yours

WhyMessages are processed on the phone, consents are listed in Profile, and “Delete all my data” is one tap. This follows the consent-first spirit of India’s DPDP Act.

Phase 03

Checking & testing

How I’ll test it with real people

Pilot
03
1

Step 01Pilot

  1. 01

    Two-week Android pilot with real bank SMS, to measure how many UPI payments are caught and categorised correctly.

  2. 02

    Compare two groups: one with the daily limit and one with a monthly budget. Measure total spending, not just one category, since a nudge on food can move spending elsewhere.

✦ What would change my mind

If people find a daily limit too strict, I’ll test a weekly limit shown day by day. If SMS access fails Play review, Account Aggregator becomes the main source and the “live” promise becomes “updated a few times a day”.

What I learned

Clarity is kinder than control

01Check the idea against data first

Public payment data and one solid study told me more than my own habits did, and showed what I couldn’t claim.

02Choose the time frame carefully

Moving from monthly to daily was the biggest design decision. It changed every screen.

03Tone is a feature

The same −₹278 can make someone close the app or make a plan. The words decide which.

04AI needs limits to be trusted

Making the assistant read-only made it easier to trust, not less useful.

Know where your money goes, while you can still change it.
